title: the butter thief

segments.voice: Yesterday, Putana: she came to the baby with poison, and the text says even she was blessed, because she had fed him like a mother. Your line was even she was blessed.

A group of women stands at Yashoda's door, and they have a list. They are the gopis, the cowherd women of the village. Putana is gone, and now there's a different problem, and he's a toddler. Butter has been disappearing all over the village. Curd too. Milk pots are broken. And every trail leads back to this house. So they come to his mother, half laughing, half fed up, and make their case, item by item.
screen: `WOMEN AT YASHODA'S DOOR.` → `BUTTER IS DISAPPEARING.` → `EVERY TRAIL LEADS HERE.`

segments.voice: Here is their list, as the Bhagavata Purana gives it. He turns the calves loose before milking time, and when someone scolds him, he laughs. He gets into the milk and curd, and when he's had his fill, he feeds the rest to the monkeys. If a monkey won't eat, he breaks the pot. People hang their pots high from the ceiling on ropes, so he drags over stools and a mortar and climbs, or makes a hole in the bottom of the pot and drinks from underneath. In a dark storeroom he doesn't even need a lamp: the jewels he wears light the way. That's the case for the prosecution. Then the turn. All the while, Krishna sits beside his mother with wide, frightened eyes, the picture of a child who has never touched a pot in his life. The women look at that face and can't keep scolding. They laugh. And Yashoda, the text says, smiles and doesn't have the heart to punish him. Notice what kind of complaint this is. Nobody stops making butter. Nobody locks the door. They keep coming to report him, and in the reporting they get to talk about him, and be near him. Some devotional teachers read the stolen butter as the heart of the devotee: the thing you hang up high, out of reach, that he finds a way into anyway. Take it that way or simply as a story about a little boy; either way, the village is full of people who keep leaving the butter out.
screen: `THE CALVES, THE MONKEYS, THE POTS.` · `STOOLS, A MORTAR, A HOLE IN THE POT.` · `THE INNOCENT FACE.` · then, large: `THEY CAN'T KEEP SCOLDING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small person you love, or the small person you once were, caught in some harmless mischief: a face covered in something sticky, a drawer emptied onto the floor. Hold the picture; there may be a little annoyance, and something warmer alongside it, and both can stay. If you pray, you can say Krishna's name, or a name for God you already use, once, quietly.
gopis. The cowherd women of the village, who bring Yashoda their long list of complaints about her butter-stealing little boy.
Your line: they can't keep scolding. Tomorrow, his mother reaches for a rope. That's day eight hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Krishna as the butter thief is a familiar figure in Hindu devotion: images of the child Krishna with butter in his hand are kept in homes and temples, and on Janmashtami some communities hang pots of curd high up for teams to climb and break.

chat.says: If Krishna kept stealing their butter, why didn't the gopis just lock it up?
options: They kept leaving it out; reporting him let them talk about him and be near him.
They did lock it up, but Yashoda gave him the keys to their storerooms.
They wanted the monkeys to eat it, so the butter would not go to waste.
chat.meaning: Nobody stops making butter or locks the door. Their complaints are a way to talk about him and be near him.

All paraphrase; no public-domain English translation is quoted. Confirm the items of the gopis' complaint (calves loosed early, feeding monkeys, breaking pots, stools and mortar, holes in hanging pots, jewels lighting dark rooms) against Bhagavata 10.8.
The text's complaint also includes cruder items (soiling clean houses) and making the children of the house cry; deliberately left out.
Review line: confirm the framing that Putana was granted a blessed end because she nursed him like a mother (Bhagavata 10.6).
